claim: The binding affinity between NAD+ and SIRT1 is within the range of -8 to -10 kcal/mol.
source: We found that the binding affinity between NAD+ and all nuclear SIRTs was within the range of –eight to –10 kcal/mol (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular docking analysis data presented in Figure 1A showing predicted binding affinities.

claim: The binding affinity between NAD+ and SIRT6 is within the range of -8 to -10 kcal/mol.
source: We found that the binding affinity between NAD+ and all nuclear SIRTs was within the range of –eight to –10 kcal/mol (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular docking analysis data presented in Figure 1A showing predicted binding affinities.

claim: The binding affinity between NAD+ and SIRT7 is within the range of -8 to -10 kcal/mol.
source: We found that the binding affinity between NAD+ and all nuclear SIRTs was within the range of –eight to –10 kcal/mol (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular docking analysis data presented in Figure 1A showing predicted binding affinities.

claim: The binding affinity between DSBs and SIRT6 is -12.7 kcal/mol.
source: Surprisingly, only the binding between the DSB and SIRT6 was energetically favored (–12.7 kcal/mol), being even lower than that of NAD+ (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular docking analysis data presented in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: The binding affinity between DSBs and SIRT6 is lower than the binding affinity between NAD+ and SIRT6.
source: Surprisingly, only the binding between the DSB and SIRT6 was energetically favored (–12.7 kcal/mol), being even lower than that of NAD+ (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular docking analysis data comparing binding affinities in Figure 1A.

claim: Recombinant SIRT6 binds to a biotin-conjugated DNA duplex in vitro.
source: Recombinant SIRT6 (rSIRT6), but not rSIRT1 or rSIRT7, bound to the DNA duplex (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by pulldown assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Recombinant SIRT1 does not bind to a biotin-conjugated DNA duplex in vitro.
source: Recombinant SIRT6 (rSIRT6), but not rSIRT1 or rSIRT7, bound to the DNA duplex (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by pulldown assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Recombinant SIRT7 does not bind to a biotin-conjugated DNA duplex in vitro.
source: Recombinant SIRT6 (rSIRT6), but not rSIRT1 or rSIRT7, bound to the DNA duplex (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by pulldown assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The Kd for the interaction between SIRT6 and a FAM-labeled DNA duplex is 166.3 nM.
source: This finding was verified by a fluorescence polarization (FP) assay using a FAM-labeled DNA duplex. We observed dynamic FP (Kd = 166.3 nM; Figure 1D), supporting a specific and direct interaction between the DNA duplex and rSIRT6.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence polarization assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: SIRT1 shows minimal fluorescence polarization with a FAM-labeled DNA duplex.
source: By contrast, the FP was minimal for rSIRT1, rSIRT7 and GST control (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence polarization assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: SIRT7 shows minimal fluorescence polarization with a FAM-labeled DNA duplex.
source: By contrast, the FP was minimal for rSIRT1, rSIRT7 and GST control (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence polarization assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Linearized DNA inhibits rSIRT6 binding to a biotin-labeled DNA duplex.
source: While linearized DNA inhibited rSIRT6 binding to the DNA duplex, circular DNA had a minimal effect (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by pulldown assay data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Circular DNA has a minimal effect on rSIRT6 binding to a biotin-labeled DNA duplex.
source: While linearized DNA inhibited rSIRT6 binding to the DNA duplex, circular DNA had a minimal effect (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by pulldown assay data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: SIRT6 directly recognizes and binds to DSBs.
source: Together, these data indicate that SIRT6, but not SIRT1 or SIRT7 recognizes and directly binds to DSBs.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experimental data including molecular docking, pulldown assays, and fluorescence polarization assays.

claim: SIRT6 forms an asymmetric hexamer.
source: As predicted from the crystallographic data, SIRT6s form an asymmetric hexamer (Pan et al., 2011) that generates three potential DSB binding pockets; each of these pockets consist of two N-termini and two C-termini from two adjacent molecules (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to crystallographic data from Pan et al., 2011 and illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The SIRT6 hexamer generates three potential DSB binding pockets.
source: As predicted from the crystallographic data, SIRT6s form an asymmetric hexamer (Pan et al., 2011) that generates three potential DSB binding pockets; each of these pockets consist of two N-termini and two C-termini from two adjacent molecules (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to crystallographic data from Pan et al., 2011 and illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Each DSB binding pocket in the SIRT6 hexamer consists of two N-termini and two C-termini from two adjacent molecules.
source: As predicted from the crystallographic data, SIRT6s form an asymmetric hexamer (Pan et al., 2011) that generates three potential DSB binding pockets; each of these pockets consist of two N-termini and two C-termini from two adjacent molecules (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to crystallographic data from Pan et al., 2011 and illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Both the N-termini and C-termini of SIRT6 are essential for its association with chromatin.
source: Both the N-termini and C-termini are essential for SIRT6 to associate with chromatin (Tennen et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tennen et al., 2010.

claim: N-SIRT6 directly interacts with C-SIRT6 in HEK293 cells as detected by BiFC assay.
source: After co-transfecting these constructs into HEK293 cells, we detected a strong fluorescence signal by FACS in >24% cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), suggesting a direct interaction between the two SIRT6 molecules.
evidence: The claim is supported by BiFC assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: FLAG-SIRT6 interacts with HA-SIRT6 in HEK293 cells.
source: To confirm this SIRT6 polymerization event, we performed co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) in HEK293 cells in which we had co-overexpressed FLAG-SIRT6 and HA-SIRT6. Consistently, we detected FLAG-SIRT6 but not FLAG-SIRT3 in the anti-HA-SIRT6 immunoprecipitates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: FLAG-SIRT3 does not interact with HA-SIRT6 in HEK293 cells.
source: To confirm this SIRT6 polymerization event, we performed co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) in HEK293 cells in which we had co-overexpressed FLAG-SIRT6 and HA-SIRT6. Consistently, we detected FLAG-SIRT6 but not FLAG-SIRT3 in the anti-HA-SIRT6 immunoprecipitates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: One predicted DSB-binding pocket in the SIRT6 hexamer consists of six positively charged residues at the edge: four arginine (R32/39) and two lysine (K33) residues.
source: Indeed, one of our predicted DSB-binding pockets formed by two adjacent molecules in SIRT6 hexamer consisted of six positively charged residues at the edge, namely four arginine (R32/39) and two lysine (K33) residues (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Acetylation converts positively charged lysine to neutral Kac.
source: Acetylation is the most redundant post-translational modification that converts positively charged K to neutral Kac.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about acetylation as a post-translational modification.

claim: Proteins with a lysine-rich domain (KRD) use acetylation to mediate dynamic interactions with proteins harboring an acidic domain.
source: This property is utilized by proteins with a lysine-rich domain (KRD), for example Histones, Ku70 and p53, for mediating dynamic interactions with proteins harboring an acidic domain like SET (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2016.

claim: The heterodimerized Ku70 and Ku80 complex directly senses DSBs via a flexible C-termini containing multiple K residues.
source: The heterodimerized Ku70 and Ku80 complex directly senses DSBs via a flexible C-termini containing multiple K residues, and regulates NHEJ (Hu et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hu et al., 2012.

claim: FLAG-SIRT6 is acetylated in HEK293 cells.
source: As shown, Kac was detected in the precipitated FLAG-SIRT6 immunocomplex (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: SIRT6 is acetylated at K15 and K33 in the N-terminus.
source: We then purified FLAG-SIRT6 and performed high-resolution LC-MS/MS to identify which K residues are acetylated (Supplementary file 1). We identified K15 and K33 in the N-terminus.
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data referenced in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The K33R mutation significantly inhibits FLAG-SIRT6 acetylation.
source: While neither K15R nor K17R affected the FLAG-SIRT6 acetylation level, K33R significantly inhibited it (Figures 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), supporting that K33 is dynamically (de)acetylated.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The K15R mutation does not affect FLAG-SIRT6 acetylation level.
source: While neither K15R nor K17R affected the FLAG-SIRT6 acetylation level, K33R significantly inhibited it (Figures 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), supporting that K33 is dynamically (de)acetylated.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The K17R mutation does not affect FLAG-SIRT6 acetylation level.
source: While neither K15R nor K17R affected the FLAG-SIRT6 acetylation level, K33R significantly inhibited it (Figures 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), supporting that K33 is dynamically (de)acetylated.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: K33 of SIRT6 is dynamically (de)acetylated.
source: While neither K15R nor K17R affected the FLAG-SIRT6 acetylation level, K33R significantly inhibited it (Figures 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), supporting that K33 is dynamically (de)acetylated.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data showing that K33R mutation reduces acetylation.

claim: SIRT6 K33Q binding to a biotin-labeled DNA duplex is significantly compromised compared to SIRT6 WT.
source: K33Q and H133Y binding to the DNA duplex was significantly compromised compared to WT and K33R binding (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by pulldown assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: SIRT6 H133Y binding to a biotin-labeled DNA duplex is significantly compromised compared to SIRT6 WT.
source: K33Q and H133Y binding to the DNA duplex was significantly compromised compared to WT and K33R binding (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by pulldown assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: SIRT6 K33R binding to a biotin-labeled DNA duplex is comparable to SIRT6 WT.
source: K33Q and H133Y binding to the DNA duplex was significantly compromised compared to WT and K33R binding (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by pulldown assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The Kd for the interaction between SIRT6 K33R and FAM-labeled DNA is 104.9 nM.
source: Consistently, we recorded notable FP for SIRT6 K33R (Kd = 104.9 nM) but little FP for SIRT6 K33Q (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence polarization assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: SIRT6 K33Q shows little fluorescence polarization with FAM-labeled DNA.
source: Consistently, we recorded notable FP for SIRT6 K33R (Kd = 104.9 nM) but little FP for SIRT6 K33Q (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence polarization assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: H133 is critical for enriching SIRT6 on chromatin.
source: H133 is critical for enriching SIRT6 on chromatin (Tennen et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tennen et al., 2010.

claim: The K33Q mutation significantly jeopardizes efficient SIRT6 recruitment to DNA breaks.
source: While the K33Q and H133Y mutations significantly jeopardized efficient SIRT6 recruitment to DNA breaks, the SIRT6 K33R mutant retained such ability (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claim: The H133Y mutation significantly jeopardizes efficient SIRT6 recruitment to DNA breaks.
source: While the K33Q and H133Y mutations significantly jeopardized efficient SIRT6 recruitment to DNA breaks, the SIRT6 K33R mutant retained such ability (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claim: The SIRT6 K33R mutant retains the ability to be recruited to DNA breaks.
source: While the K33Q and H133Y mutations significantly jeopardized efficient SIRT6 recruitment to DNA breaks, the SIRT6 K33R mutant retained such ability (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claim: The K33Q mutation compromises SIRT6 recruitment to induced DSBs in the DR-GFP reporter system.
source: Both the K33Q and H133Y mutations compromised SIRT6 recruitment to the sites of damage, whereas SIRT6 K33R recruitment was comparable to that of SIRT6 WT (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The H133Y mutation compromises SIRT6 recruitment to induced DSBs in the DR-GFP reporter system.
source: Both the K33Q and H133Y mutations compromised SIRT6 recruitment to the sites of damage, whereas SIRT6 K33R recruitment was comparable to that of SIRT6 WT (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: SIRT6 K33R recruitment to induced DSBs is comparable to SIRT6 WT in the DR-GFP reporter system.
source: Both the K33Q and H133Y mutations compromised SIRT6 recruitment to the sites of damage, whereas SIRT6 K33R recruitment was comparable to that of SIRT6 WT (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The acetylation levels of H3K9 and H3K56 decline upon DNA damage.
source: Upon DNA damage, the acetylation levels of H3K9 and H3K56 decline, and after repair, goes back to the original level (Tjeertes et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tjeertes et al., 2009.

claim: H3K9ac and H3K56ac are deacetylating targets of SIRT6.
source: H3K9ac and H3K56ac are deacetylating targets of SIRT6, indicating that SIRT6 might contribute to the reduced H3K9ac and H3K56ac levels on the DSB-surrounding chromatin.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about SIRT6 deacetylase activity.

claim: Reconstituted SIRT6 WT downregulates the levels of H3K9ac and H3K56ac in Sirt6–/– cells.
source: Indeed, reconstituted SIRT6 WT and K33R downregulated the levels of H3K9ac and H3K56ac in Sirt6–/– cells, while K33Q and H133Y failed (Figure 2I and J and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2I, 2J, and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Reconstituted SIRT6 K33R downregulates the levels of H3K9ac and H3K56ac in Sirt6–/– cells.
source: Indeed, reconstituted SIRT6 WT and K33R downregulated the levels of H3K9ac and H3K56ac in Sirt6–/– cells, while K33Q and H133Y failed (Figure 2I and J and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2I, 2J, and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: SIRT6 K33Q fails to downregulate the levels of H3K9ac and H3K56ac in Sirt6–/– cells.
source: Indeed, reconstituted SIRT6 WT and K33R downregulated the levels of H3K9ac and H3K56ac in Sirt6–/– cells, while K33Q and H133Y failed (Figure 2I and J and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2I, 2J, and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: SIRT6 H133Y fails to downregulate the levels of H3K9ac and H3K56ac in Sirt6–/– cells.
source: Indeed, reconstituted SIRT6 WT and K33R downregulated the levels of H3K9ac and H3K56ac in Sirt6–/– cells, while K33Q and H133Y failed (Figure 2I and J and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2I, 2J, and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The K33Q mutation affects SNF2H recruitment to DSBs.
source: Further, the K33Q and H133Y mutations also affected SNF2H recruitment to DSBs (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B), which requires SIRT6 (Toiber et al., 2013), but no effect was observed in the presence of the K33R mutation.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell fractionation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B and citation to Toiber et al., 2013.

claim: The H133Y mutation affects SNF2H recruitment to DSBs.
source: Further, the K33Q and H133Y mutations also affected SNF2H recruitment to DSBs (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B), which requires SIRT6 (Toiber et al., 2013), but no effect was observed in the presence of the K33R mutation.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell fractionation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B and citation to Toiber et al., 2013.

claim: The K33R mutation does not affect SNF2H recruitment to DSBs.
source: Further, the K33Q and H133Y mutations also affected SNF2H recruitment to DSBs (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B), which requires SIRT6 (Toiber et al., 2013), but no effect was observed in the presence of the K33R mutation.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell fractionation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B and citation to Toiber et al., 2013.

claim: SNF2H recruitment to DSBs requires SIRT6.
source: Further, the K33Q and H133Y mutations also affected SNF2H recruitment to DSBs (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B), which requires SIRT6 (Toiber et al., 2013), but no effect was observed in the presence of the K33R mutation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Toiber et al., 2013.

claim: Neither K33R nor K33Q affects the deacetylase activity of SIRT6.
source: Of note, neither K33R nor K33Q affected the deacetylase activity of SIRT6 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro deacetylase activity assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: HA-SIRT6 binds to FLAG-SIRT6 in HEK293 cells.
source: We co-overexpressed HA-SIRT6 and various FLAG-SIRT6 mutants and performed Co-IP. We detected FLAG-SIRT6 in the anti-HA immunoprecipitates, supporting that SIRT6 polymerization occurs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: HA-SIRT6 binds to FLAG-SIRT6 K33R in HEK293 cells.
source: While HA-SIRT6 was still able to bind to FLAG-SIRT6 K33R, its binding to SIRT6 K33Q was significantly jeopardized.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: HA-SIRT6 binding to FLAG-SIRT6 K33Q is significantly jeopardized.
source: While HA-SIRT6 was still able to bind to FLAG-SIRT6 K33R, its binding to SIRT6 K33Q was significantly jeopardized.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: The enzyme-dead H133Y mutation jeopardizes SIRT6 polymerization.
source: Of note, the enzyme-dead H133Y mutation also jeopardized SIRT6 polymerization. This finding is consistent with the fact that the H133 site is important for both SIRT6 deacetylase activity and for mediating the chromatin association (Tennen et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data and citation to Tennen et al., 2010.

claim: The H133 site is important for both SIRT6 deacetylase activity and for mediating the chromatin association.
source: Of note, the enzyme-dead H133Y mutation also jeopardized SIRT6 polymerization. This finding is consistent with the fact that the H133 site is important for both SIRT6 deacetylase activity and for mediating the chromatin association (Tennen et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tennen et al., 2010.

claim: Dynamic SIRT6 K33 (de)acetylation modulates SIRT6 polymerization and DSB binding.
source: Together, these data implicate that dynamic SIRT6 K33 (de)acetylation modulates SIRT6 polymerization and thus DSB binding.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on multiple experimental data showing effects of K33 mutations on SIRT6 polymerization and DSB binding.

claim: The level of acetylated SIRT6 is largely elevated in the presence of nicotinamide (NAM).
source: We noticed that the level of acetylated SIRT6 was largely elevated in the presence of the class III HDAC (SIRTs) inhibitor nicotinamide (NAM) or the SIRT1-specific inhibitor Ex527, but not the class I/II HADC inhibitor Trichostatin A (TSA) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The level of acetylated SIRT6 is largely elevated in the presence of Ex527.
source: We noticed that the level of acetylated SIRT6 was largely elevated in the presence of the class III HDAC (SIRTs) inhibitor nicotinamide (NAM) or the SIRT1-specific inhibitor Ex527, but not the class I/II HADC inhibitor Trichostatin A (TSA) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Trichostatin A (TSA) does not elevate the level of acetylated SIRT6.
source: We noticed that the level of acetylated SIRT6 was largely elevated in the presence of the class III HDAC (SIRTs) inhibitor nicotinamide (NAM) or the SIRT1-specific inhibitor Ex527, but not the class I/II HADC inhibitor Trichostatin A (TSA) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: FLAG-SIRT6 interacts with endogenous SIRT1 in HEK293 cells.
source: Indeed, co-IP and western blotting revealed that FLAG-SIRT6 interacted with endogenous SIRT1 (Figure 3A) and vice versa in HEK293 cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: FLAG-SIRT1 interacts with endogenous SIRT6 in HEK293 cells.
source: Indeed, co-IP and western blotting revealed that FLAG-SIRT6 interacted with endogenous SIRT1 (Figure 3A) and vice versa in HEK293 cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: SIRT1 is detected in anti-SIRT6 immunoprecipitates in HeLa cells.
source: In addition, we detected SIRT1 in the anti-SIRT6 immunoprecipitates and vice versa (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: SIRT6 is detected in anti-SIRT1 immunoprecipitates in HeLa cells.
source: In addition, we detected SIRT1 in the anti-SIRT6 immunoprecipitates and vice versa (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: His-SIRT1 directly interacts with GST-SIRT6 in vitro.
source: A GST pulldown assay confirmed that His-SIRT1 directly interacted with GST-SIRT6 (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by GST pulldown assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: GFP-SIRT6 and DsRed-SIRT1 co-localize in U2OS cells.
source: Further, we observed co-localization between SIRT6 and SIRT1 by confocal microscopy in cells co-transfected with GFP-SIRT6 and DsRed-SIRT1 or in cells co-stained with specific antibodies (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Endogenous SIRT6 and SIRT1 co-localize in cells.
source: Further, we observed co-localization between SIRT6 and SIRT1 by confocal microscopy in cells co-transfected with GFP-SIRT6 and DsRed-SIRT1 or in cells co-stained with specific antibodies (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The interaction between SIRT6 and SIRT1 is lost if the N-terminus of SIRT6 is deleted.
source: Western blotting analysis showed that the interaction between SIRT6 and SIRT1 was lost if the N-terminus or C-terminus of SIRT6 was deleted (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The interaction between SIRT6 and SIRT1 is lost if the C-terminus of SIRT6 is deleted.
source: Western blotting analysis showed that the interaction between SIRT6 and SIRT1 was lost if the N-terminus or C-terminus of SIRT6 was deleted (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The C-terminus of SIRT6 contains the nuclear location signal.
source: As the C-terminus contains the nuclear location signal (Tennen et al., 2010), we speculate that its depletion may restrict SIRT6 in cytoplasm, thus preventing the interaction between SIRT1 and SIRT6.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tennen et al., 2010.

claim: SIRT6 physically interacts with SIRT1, most likely through the N-terminus of SIRT6.
source: Thus, the data indicate that SIRT6 physically interacts with SIRT1, most likely through the N-terminus of SIRT6.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on co-immunoprecipitation data showing that N-terminus deletion abolishes the interaction.

claim: Overexpression of SIRT1 inhibits FLAG-SIRT6 acetylation.
source: Overexpression of SIRT1 but not of other sirtuins inhibited FLAG-SIRT6 acetylation (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Overexpression of SIRT2 does not inhibit FLAG-SIRT6 acetylation.
source: Overexpression of SIRT1 but not of other sirtuins inhibited FLAG-SIRT6 acetylation (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Knocking down SIRT1 significantly upregulates endogenous SIRT6 acetylation in HEK293 cells.
source: Conversely, knocking down SIRT1 significantly upregulated endogenous SIRT6 acetylation in HEK293 cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The SIRT6 acetylation level decreases in the presence of ectopic SIRT1.
source: Furthermore, the SIRT6 acetylation level decreased in the presence of ectopic SIRT1 but not in the presence of its catalytic mutant SIRT1-H363Y (Figure 4C), despite the two proteins still showing a physical interaction, suggesting that SIRT6 is likely a deacetylation target of SIRT1.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The SIRT6 acetylation level does not decrease in the presence of SIRT1-H363Y.
source: Furthermore, the SIRT6 acetylation level decreased in the presence of ectopic SIRT1 but not in the presence of its catalytic mutant SIRT1-H363Y (Figure 4C), despite the two proteins still showing a physical interaction, suggesting that SIRT6 is likely a deacetylation target of SIRT1.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: SIRT1 and SIRT1-H363Y both show a physical interaction with SIRT6.
source: Furthermore, the SIRT6 acetylation level decreased in the presence of ectopic SIRT1 but not in the presence of its catalytic mutant SIRT1-H363Y (Figure 4C), despite the two proteins still showing a physical interaction, suggesting that SIRT6 is likely a deacetylation target of SIRT1.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data.

claim: SIRT6 is likely a deacetylation target of SIRT1.
source: Furthermore, the SIRT6 acetylation level decreased in the presence of ectopic SIRT1 but not in the presence of its catalytic mutant SIRT1-H363Y (Figure 4C), despite the two proteins still showing a physical interaction, suggesting that SIRT6 is likely a deacetylation target of SIRT1.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on data showing that SIRT1 but not its catalytic mutant reduces SIRT6 acetylation.

claim: SIRT1 deacetylates SIRT6 in the presence of NAD+ in vitro.
source: We found that SIRT1 deacetylated SIRT6 in the presence of NAD+, while NAM inhibited this process (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro deacetylation assay data shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: NAM inhibits SIRT1-mediated deacetylation of SIRT6 in vitro.
source: We found that SIRT1 deacetylated SIRT6 in the presence of NAD+, while NAM inhibited this process (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro deacetylation assay data shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: The deacetylase-inactive SIRT1-H363Y is unable to deacetylate SIRT6.
source: The deacetylase-inactive SIRT1-H363Y was unable to deacetylate SIRT6.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro deacetylation assay data.

claim: The acetylation level of SIRT6 is increased in SIRT1–/– HEK293 cells.
source: While the acetylation level of SIRT6 was increased in SIRT1–/– HEK293 cells, that of K33R was hardly affected (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The acetylation level of SIRT6 K33R is hardly affected in SIRT1–/– HEK293 cells.
source: While the acetylation level of SIRT6 was increased in SIRT1–/– HEK293 cells, that of K33R was hardly affected (Figure 4F).
